title: Tummy Time: Back to Sleep, Tummy to Play
hook: The same babies who must sleep on their backs need time on their tummies while awake — it builds the strength behind rolling and crawling, and helps keep the back of the head from flattening.
key_points: Start tummy time from the first days: short, supervised sessions while the baby is awake, a few times a day.
Build up gradually toward 15–30 minutes a day in total by around 3–4 months, in shorter bursts.
It strengthens the neck, shoulders, and core — the foundation for rolling, sitting, and crawling.
It also reduces flat spots on the head (positional plagiocephaly) that can come from time spent on the back.
content_html: Safe sleep means a baby is always on their back — but a baby who only ever lies on their back misses out on important development. The fix is tummy time: placing your baby on their stomach while they're awake and you're watching. The catchphrase pediatricians use sums it up: "back to sleep, tummy to play."
extra_html: You can begin in the first days with very short sessions, a few times a day, working up to a total of roughly 15 to 30 minutes daily by three or four months — done in short bursts rather than one long stretch. Lying on the tummy is hard work for a baby, and that effort is the point: it strengthens the neck, shoulders, and core that later power rolling, sitting, and crawling. As a bonus, varying a baby's position helps prevent the flat spots on the back of the head (positional plagiocephaly) that can develop from lots of time lying down. If your baby protests at first, start small, get down at eye level, and make it playful. This is general educational information from the AAP.

related.title: Motor Milestones: Rolling to Crawling
related.hook: In the first year babies move through a rough sequence — rolling, sitting, crawling, pulling to stand — but the timing varies widely, and ranges matter more than exact dates.

related.title: Always Put a Baby to Sleep on Their Back
related.hook: Placing healthy babies on their back for every sleep — naps and night — is the single most effective step to reduce the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).

flashcards.prompt: When is tummy time appropriate, given the back-to-sleep rule?

choices.text: While the baby is awake and supervised — 'back to sleep, tummy to play'
Only during naps and overnight sleep
Not until the baby can already roll over

flashcards.explanation_html: Babies sleep on their backs, but they need supervised tummy time while awake. The phrase is 'back to sleep, tummy to play.'

flashcards.prompt: What two things does regular tummy time help with?
flashcards.back_html: It builds neck, shoulder, and core strength for rolling, sitting, and crawling — and it reduces flat spots on the back of the head (plagiocephaly).
